situation.note: replaying a conversation from 2019 at 2am again. I know it doesn't matter. my brain won't let it go.

understanding.bridge: The 2am replay you cannot stop is what the Upanishads call the untrained mind: running like the wind, and left to itself it becomes its own enemy.
understanding.week_thesis: The 2am replay has a name, and the mind has a way out that does not require forgetting.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the replaying and the exhaustion, named without blame.
week_beats.diagnose: You see that the mind is doing what untrained minds do: it reopens the past and calls it present.
week_beats.steady: You hold that the mind is not your fault, and that it can be steadied.
week_beats.act: You try letting the thought come, letting it go, and returning to the breath, one time at a time.
week_beats.story: A young seeker who could not still their mind, who sat with a teacher and learned that the mind's restlessness is not their fault.

understanding.mirror: You know it doesn't matter, and am your mind says it does anyway.
understanding.insight: The conversation is from years ago, and your mind has never been given one quiet minute to settle since.

queries.hook: The weight of a mind that will not let go of something you know does not matter, and the exhaustion of replaying it am.
queries.diagnose: A mind that runs like the wind, replaying and imagining, becomes its own enemy when left to itself; it turns the past into a present it cannot close.
queries.steady: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong; holding it feels like holding the wind, and that is not your failure.
queries.act: Practise steadying the mind; let the thought come, let it go, and return your attention to the breath, one time at a time.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse.sanskrit: यतो यतो निश्चरति मनश्चञ्चलमस्थिरम् । ततस्ततो नियम्यैतदात्मन्येव वशं नयेत् ॥
verse.line: Wherever the restless mind wanders, gently bring it back. Again and again.
verse.translation: Wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders, from there one should draw it back and bring it under the control of the self.
verse.why: Moderation and gentle return, again and again, settle the mind.

matched.label: I can't sleep, my mind is racing

prasang.title: Meditation in detail
prasang.summary: Krishna describes meditation: moderation in food and sleep, the mind like a lamp in a windless place, bringing the wandering mind back, and feeling others' joy and pain as one's own.
prasang.lesson: Moderation and gentle return, again and again, settle the mind.

verse.meaning: Krishna is teaching Arjuna how to meditate. He tells Arjuna that the mind will wander. It will run to old memories and new fears. The mind will not stay still on its own. Krishna says to take the mind wherever it goes. Gently pull it back to the place of focus. Do this again and again. It is a slow work. The mind does not settle in one day. It is a practice of returning, not a battle of forcing.
verse.for_you: Your mind is running a conversation from years ago. You know it does not matter. Still, it replays. The tiredness you feel is the work of pulling it back. You do not need to win the fight. You could return, again and again. The mind is a restless animal.
verse.scene_line: You are sitting with a mind that will not sit still.
asks: How do I bring the mind back without anger?
What is the one thing I can bring it to?

verse.speaker: Rama
verse.setting: Rama, near the end of his lament, says where the real enemy lives.
verse.sanskrit: शत्रवश्चेन्द्रियाण्येव सत्यं यातमसत्यताम् । प्रहरत्यात्मनैवात्मा मनसैव मनो रिपुः ॥
verse.line: No one hurts us like we hurt ourselves. The mind becomes the mind's own enemy.
verse.translation: Our own senses are the enemies; truth itself has turned untrue; the self strikes the self, and the mind is the mind's own enemy.
verse.why: Naming honestly what feels empty is the first step; Rama's lament is a question, not the answer.
verse.misuse: Not a reason to blame yourself. Vasishtha's answer is that the same mind can lift itself.

prasang.title: Rama's lament: what is the point of all this?
prasang.summary: Asked to speak, Rama pours out what he has seen: wealth hardens people, life drips away like water off a leaf, ego and craving run us, the mind never fills, childhood, youth and old age each bring their own suffering, and time eats everything. He ends by saying only the company of good people gives him hope.
prasang.story_hook: In front of the whole court, the young prince stood up and said what everyone feels and nobody says.
prasang.lesson: Naming honestly what feels empty is the first step; Rama's lament is a question, not the answer.

verse.meaning: Rama, near the end of his grief, asks the sages where the real enemy lives. He says our own senses are the enemies, truth itself has turned untrue, the self strikes the self, and the mind is the mind's own enemy. He is naming honestly what feels empty and hollow inside. He is not offering the answer yet. He is simply pointing to the place where the wound is, without turning away from it.
verse.for_you: That conversation from years ago is not the enemy. Your own mind is turning it into a fight it can never win. You are not broken for replaying it. You are simply tired of your own attention keeping the door open.
verse.try_today: When the replay starts, name it as your own mind's work, not as a fact about the past.
verse.scene_line: You are listening to your own mind turn the past into a battle it can never win.
asks: How do I see my mind as the one doing the replaying?
What is the difference between my mind and the thoughts it produces?

verse.speaker: Yama
verse.sanskrit: यस्त्वविज्ञानवान्भवत्ययुक्तेन मनसा सदा । तस्येन्द्रियाण्यवश्यानि दुष्टाश्वा इव सारथेः ॥ यस्तु विज्ञानवान्भवति युक्तेन मनसा सदा । तस्येन्द्रियाणि वश्यानि सदश्वा इव सारथेः ॥
verse.line: Without understanding, the senses bolt like wild horses; with a steady mind, they run like trained ones.
verse.translation: For one who lacks understanding, whose mind is never held steady, the senses run out of control like a driver's wild horses. For one who has understanding, whose mind is always steady, the senses obey like good horses.
verse.why: Hold the reins of your mind, or your senses will drive for you.

prasang.title: The chariot of the self
prasang.summary: Yama pictures a person as a chariot: the self is the rider, the body the chariot, the intellect the driver, the mind the reins and the senses the horses. With a steady mind the horses obey; without it they bolt. He ends with the call to arise and wake.
prasang.lesson: Hold the reins of your mind, or your senses will drive for you.

verse.meaning: Yama is still speaking to Nachiketa, who has refused the world to learn what happens after death. He continues with the chariot. The body is the chariot, the intellect is the driver, the mind is the reins, and the senses are the horses. When the mind is unsteady, the senses run wild and the rider is dragged where they will. When the mind is steady, the senses follow the driver and the rider reaches their goal. The verse says that without understanding, the senses bolt like wild horses.
verse.for_you: That conversation from years ago is not the chariot driver. It is the wild horse. You are the rider, and the reins are in your hands right now. You are not failing because the mind is loud. You are simply not yet holding the reins.
verse.scene_line: You are the rider, and the reins are in your hands.
asks: How do I hold the reins when the mind is tired?

verse.speaker: Bhushunda
verse.setting: Bhushunda, the ancient crow who has watched the ages pass, tells Vasishtha why he lives long and well.
verse.sanskrit: न भूतं न भविष्यं च चिन्तयामि कदाचन । दृष्टिमालम्ब्य तिष्ठामि वर्तमानामिहात्मना ॥
verse.line: I don't brood over the past or the future. I keep my attention on now.
verse.translation: I never brood over the past or the future. I hold my attention on the present, here, with myself.
verse.why: A long, steady life comes from a mind that stays in the present, wants little and stays kind.

prasang.title: Bhushunda, the crow who outlived the ages
prasang.summary: Vasishtha travels to a wish-fulfilling tree on Mount Meru to meet Bhushunda, a crow who has watched world-ages come and go. Asked how he has lived so long, untroubled, Bhushunda lists his habits: he doesn't brood on the past or future, doesn't fret about what he'll get next, doesn't grow arrogant from knowing, and shares in others' joys and sorrows.
prasang.story_hook: High on a mountain lived a crow who had watched whole ages of the world rise and fall.
prasang.lesson: A long, steady life comes from a mind that stays in the present, wants little and stays kind.

verse.meaning: Bhushunda, the ancient crow who has watched the ages pass, tells Vasishtha why he lives long and well. He says he never broods over the past or the future. He holds his attention on the present, here, with himself. A long, steady life comes from a mind that stays in the present, wants little and stays kind. The mind has a way out that does not require forgetting the conversation. It requires only this: to stop giving the past and future the power to pull the mind away from now.
verse.for_you: The replay is not a failure of your character. It is the untrained mind doing exactly what it does when left alone with a phone and a past conversation. You do not need to force the thought away.
verse.try_today: When the mind returns to the conversation, notice the room around you instead.
verse.scene_line: You are the crow on the mountain, asked how to live long and well.
asks: How do I stop the mind from wandering back?
Can I really hold my attention on now?

verse.speaker: Ribhu
verse.setting: Ribhu on inner stillness in an active life.
verse.sanskrit: बहिःकृत्रिमसंरंभो हृदि संरम्भवर्जितः । कर्ता बहिरकर्तान्तर्लोके विहर शुद्धधीः ॥
verse.line: Be busy on the outside and unhurried inside. Act fully, but don't let it agitate you.
verse.translation: Outwardly busy, inwardly free of agitation; a doer on the outside, a non-doer within: move through the world with a clear mind.
verse.why: Live fully in the world while staying unhurried inside.

prasang.title: How a free person lives
prasang.summary: Ribhu describes how a free person lives among others: letting go of what is lost, taking up what comes, doing the work at hand, speaking gently, busy outside and calm inside, and treating the whole world as family.
prasang.lesson: Live fully in the world while staying unhurried inside.

verse.meaning: Ribhu is speaking to Nidagha, a householder, explaining how a free person lives. Ribhu says a person can be outwardly busy and inwardly calm. They do the work that comes to them. They speak gently. They do not let the world shake them. The mind stays clear. The person does not let the outside world agitate the inside. They move through the world with a steady mind.
verse.for_you: Your mind has been running the same conversation for years. You are busy with work, but inside you are not calm. The outside world is fine. The trouble is inside. The way out is not to force the thought away.
verse.try_today: Let the thought come, and then return your attention to the next small task.
verse.scene_line: You are busy with work, but your mind is still in that old conversation.
asks: How do I let the thought come without letting it take over?
How do I stop the mind from making the past my present?

verse.speaker: Beings of the sky
verse.setting: Having outwitted two monsters mid-flight, Hanuman is praised by those watching from the sky.
verse.sanskrit: यस्य त्वेतानि चत्वारि वानरेन्द्र यथा तव। धृतिर्दृष्टिर्मतिर्दाक्ष्य स कर्मसु न सीदति ॥
verse.line: Steadiness, clear sight, good judgement and skill. With these four, you won't sink at work.
verse.translation: Whoever has these four, as you do, chief of monkeys, never sinks in his work: steadiness, clear sight, judgement and skill.
verse.why: Gratitude and focus can go together; know when to be big and when to be small.

prasang.title: Hanuman's leap
prasang.summary: Hanuman leaps across the ocean. A mountain rises to repay an old kindness by offering rest; he thanks it but keeps his promise not to stop. He outwits Surasa by shrinking small and defeats Simhika, and the watching beings praise his steadiness, sight, judgement and skill.
prasang.story_hook: Halfway across the ocean, a golden mountain rose out of the water and offered him a place to rest.
prasang.lesson: Gratitude and focus can go together; know when to be big and when to be small.

verse.meaning: After Hanuman shrinks to slip past the monster Surasa and then outwits the other monster Simhika, the beings watching from the sky praise him. They say that whoever has steadiness, clear sight, good judgement and skill never sinks in their work. Hanuman had the whole world on his shoulders, yet he knew how to be small when he needed to and how to stay focused without letting the weight crush him. The verse says that these four qualities are enough to keep you from sinking, no matter how large the task.
verse.for_you: Your mind is replaying a conversation from years ago while you sit with your phone for hours, and it is exhausting you. The mind is doing exactly what you fear: it is becoming its own enemy. But steadiness is not about forgetting that talk.
verse.try_today: When the replay starts, let it run for one minute, then name one thing you can see right now.
verse.scene_line: You are the sky watching yourself shrink and then leap, steady, clear, and still in motion.
asks: How do I know when to be small and when to be big?

story.title: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
story.story_hook: One spring morning, a king out for a walk overheard a song that he could not stop thinking about.
story.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to the day's work, he decides not to run away: he gets up and does his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutches.
story.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

anchor.speaker: Janaka
anchor.setting: King Janaka, alone on his palace roof after overhearing wandering sages, rethinks his life.
anchor.sanskrit: संपदश्च विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेच्चित्तेन संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा हन्त मन्ये महापदः ॥ आपदोऽपि विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेन्मनसि संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा मन्ये मनसि संपदः ॥
anchor.line: Good fortune the mind clutches becomes trouble. Trouble the mind accepts becomes a kind of fortune.
anchor.translation: All those dazzling fortunes, if the mind clings to them, are really great calamities in grand disguise. And all those varied misfortunes, if the mind accepts them, are really fortunes.
anchor.why: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.
anchor.misuse: Accepting a hardship doesn't mean not fixing what can be fixed.
